newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Edison shares suffer from ENI/Enel link.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Edison shares suffer from ENI/Enel link.

text.p: Shares in Edison, Italy's largest non state-owned producer of electricity, fell over five percent on the Milan bourse on Wednesday, after a link-up between two state energy giants.

Edison, energy subsidiary of agrichemical group Montedison, suffered for the second day running after news that state controlled energy group ENI and electricity utility Enel plan to set up Italy's largest independent electricity production firm.

ENI and Enel said on Monday they had signed a letter of intent to create a new enterprise before the end of 1997 to produce cut-price electricity aimed at domestic and foreign markets and to be listed on major international stock exchanges.

Shares in Edison, which is also Italy's largest non-state producer of natural gas, dropped three percent on Tuesday and on Wednesay dipped a further 6.7 percent before pulling back to end 5.29 percent down at 8250 lire.
But analysts said the stock market sales were overdone.

John Stewart at brokers Centrosim here called the reaction "hysterical", saying due to existing laws Edison would continue to benefit for many years from advantageous tariffs, well above average market rates.
Paola Toschi at brokers Milla also called the move a little overdone since it would take several years before Edison profits felt the effect of the new competitor.
"At the moment, there is only a letter of intent between ENI and Enel, while Edison will continue to sell for many years at pre-fixed prices," Toschi said.
Stewart confirmed a buy recommendation on Edison stock while Toschi had advised clients to lighten positions on both Edison and Sondel, a smaller private Italian utility.
Stewart said in theory Sondel should ultimately be penalised more heavily than Edison as it did not have its own gas production.
Sondel shares slid 5.49 percent to 2875 lire. Dealers noted it had been buoyed for some of the day by news it would pay a dividend in 1996 after two years without one.
Marco Opipari, analyst at Milan brokers Intersim, said the ENI/Enel link-up had created a great deal of uncertainty in the market place about the future of Edison.
He said from a strategic point of view a project to supply gas to ENI's gas subsidiary Snam could be at risk, if the new company was capable of supplying all Snam's needs on its own.
From a stock market point of view, the presence of another competitor would induce investors to switch part of their portfolio out of Edison, he said.
However Opipari also doubted Edison would feel the effect of the potential competition on its profits before 1998.
